specPoints.text: identify common materials which are electrical conductors or insulators, including metals and plastics (physics only)

primer.text: Whether charge can move through a material decides everything about how it behaves in a circuit. Metals brim with delocalised electrons and conduct freely; plastics, rubber, glass and wood have no free charges and block the flow. This note sorts the everyday materials and explains the atomic picture behind the split.

lessons.title: Conductors & delocalised electrons
lessons.opening: Metals conduct because their outermost electrons are not attached to any single atom: they form a mobile crowd around the positive ions. Since current is a flow of electrons, the freer that crowd moves, the better the metal conducts. Silver, copper, aluminium and steel are the everyday examples.
keyPoints: A conductor lets charge, usually electrons, flow through it easily.
Typical conductors are metals: silver, copper, aluminium and steel.
Metal lattices hold positive ions surrounded by delocalised outer electrons.
Those free electrons make metals good conductors, since current is a flow of electrons.
Plastics and rubbers are insulators — no free charges — so they sheath cables safely.

low.restatement: Metals conduct because their electrons are free to move; the metal ions themselves stay put.
low.analogy: A crowd in a stadium: the seats (ions) never move, but the spectators (electrons) can shuffle along the rows.
low.examPointer: Name four conducting metals if asked to identify common conductors.

medium.restatement: Conductivity is a statement about charge carriers: the more mobile the delocalised electrons, the larger the current a given push produces.
medium.analogy: A motorway versus lanes of parked cars — the freer the traffic, the bigger the flow for the same speed limit.
medium.examPointer: Tie the atomic picture to the definition: delocalised electrons are why the current flows.

check.stem: In a metal lattice the outermost electrons are:

options.explanation: The outer electrons detach from single atoms and roam the lattice.

check.stem: Current in a metal is the flow of:

options.explanation: Protons are fixed in the nuclei.

check.stem: The better the electrons move through a metal, the:

options.explanation: Mobility helps conduction, not hinders it.
Current is electron flow, so freer electrons mean better conduction.
Temperature is not what varies here.
Lattice vibration is unrelated to the electron mobility claim.

check.modelAnswer: The outer metal electrons that are not bound to any one ion and can move through the lattice.

check.stem: Explain why plastics are used to sheath mains cables.
check.modelAnswer: Plastics are insulators with no free charges, so the sheath stops the live conductor inside from delivering a shock to anyone touching the cable.

check.stem: A cable must carry current to a garden shed outdoors. Choose the conductor for the core and the insulator for the sheath, and justify both.
check.modelAnswer: Copper for the core, because it is a metal packed with free electrons; plastic for the sheath, because with no free charges it blocks the current from reaching the user.

lessons.title: Insulators & static build-up
lessons.opening: An insulator holds its charges hostage: with nothing free to move, any charge deposited on its surface stays where it landed. Rubber, plastic, glass and wood all behave this way. That immobility sounds like a weakness, but it is exactly what lets insulators hold a static charge — and what makes them safe sheaths.
keyPoints: An insulator has no free charges, so charge cannot travel through it easily.
Rubber, plastic, glass and wood are everyday insulators.
Some non-metals conduct a little in the form of static electricity.
Charge can gather on insulator surfaces and pass across when two of them touch.

low.restatement: Insulators have no free charges, so charge stays where it is put on their surfaces.
low.analogy: A parking lot with no exits: cars (charge) can enter but cannot drive through.
low.examPointer: Insulators are not 'nothing happens' materials — they hold static charge, which matters later in this topic.

medium.restatement: The absence of mobile carriers explains both safety uses (sheathing) and static phenomena (charge accumulating on surfaces).
medium.analogy: A sponge that cannot drip: whatever water lands on it, stays on it, until something touches it.
medium.examPointer: Quote the everyday insulators: rubber, plastic, glass, wood.

That describes a conductor.

Copper conducts.
Steel conducts.
All four lack free charges.
Silver and aluminium conduct.

check.stem: Charge built up on an insulator surface escapes mainly when:

options.explanation: Heating is not the escape route described.
Melting destroys the sample rather than passing charge.

options.explanation: Contact lets the gathered charge be conducted away.
Wood is the insulator of the pair.

options.explanation: Poor conductors still pass some charge as static electricity.

check.stem: Two charged insulators touch. The charge between them:

options.explanation: Contact lets the surface charge be conducted away, at least in part.
Charge is conserved, not created.
Touching does not flip the sign.
Some charge passes on contact.

check.modelAnswer: A material with no free charges that does not let charge flow through it easily.

check.stem: In what form can charge pass through a poor conductor such as wood?
check.modelAnswer: As static electricity — charge gathering on the surface and passing across on contact.

check.stem: Explain why rubbing two insulators charges them but rubbing two metals does not.
check.modelAnswer: On insulators the transferred charge stays put on each surface because nothing free can carry it away; on metals any transferred charge would flow away at once through the delocalised electrons.

check.stem: A charged plastic rod picks up small paper circles. Explain the role of the rod being an insulator.
check.modelAnswer: The rubbed surface keeps its gathered charge because the plastic has no free charges; that stationary surface charge then attracts the neutral paper.

glossary.definition: A material that lets charge flow through it easily; metals are the everyday examples.
A material with no free charges, so charge cannot travel through it easily.
Metal outer electrons free to move through the lattice — the carriers of the current.
Charge held on an insulator's surface, able to pass across only on contact.
